drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What is the main eye problem: pain, redness, vision loss, double vision, flashes or floaters, discharge, or an injury?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main eye complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: When did this start, and is it getting better, worse, or staying the same?
questions.rationale: Sudden vision change is more urgent than gradual change.

questions.text: Is it one eye or both, and did it start suddenly or over days to weeks?
questions.rationale: Unilateral sudden loss suggests vascular, retinal, or acute glaucoma causes.

questions.text: Have you lost vision, is it complete or a curtain or shadow, and can you still see light?
questions.rationale: Pattern of loss helps separate retinal detachment, vascular occlusion, and optic nerve disease.

questions.text: Have you seen flashes of light, a shower of new floaters, or a curtain over part of your vision?
questions.rationale: These symptoms raise concern for retinal tear or detachment.

questions.text: Is the eye painful, red, or sensitive to light?
questions.rationale: Painful red eye with photophobia can be keratitis, uveitis, or acute glaucoma.

questions.text: Is there severe eye pain with headache, nausea, and a cloudy or steamy cornea or halo lights?
questions.rationale: This cluster suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma, which is time-sensitive.

questions.text: Is there discharge, crusting, or is the eye stuck shut in the morning?
questions.rationale: Discharge pattern helps separate conjunctivitis from more serious infection.

questions.text: Do you wear contact lenses, sleep in them, or swim in them?
questions.rationale: Contact lens use raises risk of sight-threatening keratitis.

questions.text: Did something hit the eye, or did a chemical, metal, or dust get in it?
questions.rationale: Chemical burns and penetrating injury need immediate care.

questions.text: Do you feel like something is still in the eye, or is there a visible cut or object?
questions.rationale: A retained foreign body or globe injury changes management.

questions.text: Do you have double vision, and is it worse looking one direction or with both eyes open?
questions.rationale: Binocular diplopia can indicate cranial nerve palsy or orbital disease.

questions.text: Are the eyelids swollen, and can you still move the eye without pain?
questions.rationale: Pain with eye movement and lid swelling raise concern for orbital cellulitis.

questions.text: If you are over 50, do you have new headache, scalp tenderness, or jaw pain when chewing with the vision change?
questions.rationale: This pattern suggests giant cell arteritis.

questions.text: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or a drooping lid with the vision change?
questions.rationale: Eye symptoms plus focal neuro signs suggest stroke or aneurysm.

questions.text: Do you have diabetes, high blood pressure, autoimmune disease, or recent shingles?
questions.rationale: Systemic disease drives many acute vision threats.

questions.text: Have you had eye surgery, glaucoma, lazy eye, or retinal problems before?
questions.rationale: Prior eye disease frames the current complaint.

questions.text: Do you take blood thinners, steroids, or medicines for glaucoma or erectile dysfunction?
questions.rationale: Some drugs affect bleeding, pressure, or optic nerves.

questions.text: Do you wear glasses, and has your prescription changed quickly?
questions.rationale: Rapid refractive shift can occur with diabetes or cataract.

questions.text: Do you weld, grind metal, or work with chemicals without eye protection?
questions.rationale: Occupational injury is a common cause of acute eye complaints.

questions.text: Has anyone around you had pink eye, or have you had a recent cold?
questions.rationale: Viral conjunctivitis is often preceded by URI or sick contacts.

questions.text: Is this your only seeing eye, or is vision already limited in the other eye?
questions.rationale: Threat to a remaining good eye raises urgency.

questions.text: Is this affecting driving, reading, or work?
questions.rationale: Functional impact guides urgency, especially monocular patients.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Sudden vision loss
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes?

red_flags.label: Flashes, floaters, or curtain over vision
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe flashes, a shower of floaters, or a curtain or shadow over part of the vision?

red_flags.label: Possible acute glaucoma
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report severe eye pain with nausea, halos, or a cloudy cornea?

red_flags.label: Chemical or penetrating eye injury
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a chemical in the eye, metal striking the eye, or a cut or object in the eye?

red_flags.label: Possible orbital cellulitis
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report eyelid swelling with pain moving the eye, fever, or trouble opening the eye?

red_flags.label: New double vision
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report new double vision, especially with a drooping lid or neurologic symptoms?

red_flags.label: Possible giant cell arteritis
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does a patient over 50 report vision change with new headache, scalp tenderness, or jaw pain on chewing?
